1.1: 1.1 Ramathaim Sophim, of the mountain, etc. Origen, homily on Elcana. Or Armathaim, as it is in other codices, etc., up to 'in which the nobility of all virtues is known to bear fruit.' The same. He had two wives, etc., up to 'let us pray for this offspring, in imitation of Anna, as she herself did.' Rabanus, on the books of Kings. First the generation of the historical prophecy is to be told, etc., up to 'while her sister rejoiced in the number of her offspring.' Jerome, book on Hebrew Names. Elcana, allegorically, 'possession of God,' who is the Son of God, saying: 'The Lord possessed me': who is well 'one man,' not in number, but because he is never changed, nor otherwise made God from himself. Armathaim Sophim, 'lofty places' or 'watchtower,' this is the Jerusalem above; coming from it, he taught the watching, and by his death made us possess it. Jeroham, 'merciful.' Eliu, 'my God.' Thohu, 'sealed.' Suph, 'pouring out,' because coming to us through mercy, sealed in the passion, he said: 'My God, my God' (Matthew 27), where emptying himself he poured himself out, hence: 'Your name is oil poured out' (Song of Songs 1), poured out from his invisible things to our visible ones. Ephrathite, 'fruitful,' because he abounds with the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Ephrathite from Ephrata, wife of Caleb, or from the city Ephrata, which was afterward called Bethlehem, or from Ephraim, as some say, because he was from Ramatha, a city of Ephraim, which is situated on mount Sophim, which mountain is in the tribe of Ephraim. Gregory, on the books of Kings. Phenenna is the synagogue, which, second, first begot sons to God through the law, but now remains barren because of unbelief. Anna is the barren Church of the Gentiles, which was once barren of spiritual offspring, now redeemed by the grace of Christ. For Anna, which is interpreted 'grace,' begets sons to God through baptism and the Holy Spirit. Silo. It is at the ninetieth milestone from Neapolis in the region of Athabit.
1.3: 1.3 Priests of the Lord. Gregory, same place. How are they priests of the Lord, who below are called sons of Belial? At that time they were called priests of the Lord when the priests of idols were reckoned by the names of false gods, so that by this mark they might be distinguished from them. For by these words their faith, not their life, is declared, because they practiced wickedness of work, but did not err in faith in the Creator. Ophni, 'unshod,' or 'madness of conversion.' Phinees. Origen, homily on Elcana. 'Mute mouth' signifies the scribes and Pharisees, etc., up to 'rightly then they were dismissed and abandoned by God.'
1.4: 1.4 So the day came and Elcana offered sacrifice and gave to Phenenna, etc. Jerome, book of Hebrew Traditions. These portions are understood as garments, which on the three festivals, namely Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles, according to the custom of that people, were given to wives, children and servants. To Anna, however, he gave one portion, sad, because she had no sons to whom to give more. To Phenenna, that is the synagogue, and her sons, he gave portions, that is, temporal goods, according to the saying: 'He gave them the regions of the nations' (Psalm 104). And because the oracles of God were first entrusted to them, to Anna, that is, the Church of the Gentiles, he gave one portion, namely natural ability. Well he says: Sad, because the Lord had shut up her womb; for the time had not yet come to have mercy on her, that she might be made fruitful with spiritual grace. As Phenenna despised Anna, so the synagogue despised the Gentile world. Many of the Gentiles awaited the coming of the Redeemer, as we find in Job, and because they persevered in prayer, at last the Redeemer applied consolation to Anna, weeping and not taking food, saying:
1.8: 1.8 Anna, why do you weep? Better to the Church is her husband, that is Christ, than ten sons whom she bore from the synagogue, for she loves Christ, that is his grace, more at times than those whom she bore carnally.
1.14: 1.14 And he said to her. Septuagint. How long will you be drunk? Man sees the face, God the heart. Heli judged her drunk, who looked only at the mouth: but the Lord looked on her prayer, who saw her heart. Here a form of praying is handed down to us, that we pray not with much speaking but in compunction of heart and the pouring out of tears: because the sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit, a contrite heart, etc.
1.17: 1.17 Heli said, Go in peace, etc. And the woman went her way, etc. Do you see the woman's faith? Before she received what she had asked, she was so confident as if she had already received it. The reason was that she had prayed with much fervor, without any hesitation. She went away with a tranquil mind, as though she had obtained all. Moreover God had already shaken all anxiety from her mind, about to grant what she asked. Let us imitate this woman, and in all afflictions flee to God. If we have no children, let us ask them of him, and if we receive them, let us bring them up with much care, etc.
1.18: 1.18 And her countenance was no more changed into different things. Rabanus, on the books of Kings. Another translation: Her face fell no more, because she most surely believed herself heard. The same. For the Church was never changed by declining in different directions from the faith and love of the Redeemer.
1.19: 1.19 And the Lord remembered her. The same. Because Anna devoutly asked the Lord, she conceived and bore. So the Church, praying by natural understanding, conceived the mystery of the incarnation in her heart, bore it by the mouth of confession. And they worshiped. Origen, as above. She is not found praying in this canticle, etc., up to 'but if he lets down, Amalec, the enemy of God, conquers.'
1.20: 1.20 And she called his name Samuel. That is, God. The firstborn of Anna a prophet. Who is this but the Lord's man? Rabanus. Samuel, 'asking of God,' or his name: the author of his birth, namely, God, because to the barren woman praying he granted a son who should serve him in the temple all his days. The same. The Church from the nations, etc., up to 'when with perfect faith in the incarnation she joined herself to the primitive Church from the Jews.'
1.23: 1.23 And I pray that the Lord fulfil. What you vowed, or his own which he promised through Heli when he said: May God grant you your petition, etc. So the woman remained and nursed her son until she weaned him. And she brought him. Anna does not wish to bring the boy to the house of God before he is weaned: because the Church advances no one to the priesthood while he is a sharer in the milk of infancy, not capable of solid food and spiritual understanding. Jerome, book of Hebrew Traditions, on the books of Kings. In the Hebrew: A measure of flour, but it has been corrupted by the fault of scribes. For if with three calves she offered three measures of flour, she acted against the law, in which it is said: 'One calf from the herd, one ram, seven spotless lambs of a year; in their sacrifices of fine flour sprinkled with oil, three tenths for each calf, two tenths for the ram, one tenth for the lamb.' This tenth was the tenth part of an ephah. From which it is understood that Elcana did not offer three measures of flour with three calves, but nine tenths.
2.1: 2.1 My heart is enlarged. Rabanus. Because the word of God is not bound in pressures, not bound in the heralds. The same. In Christ, whom old Simeon embraces as a child and recognizes as great, saying: 'Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace. Because my eyes have seen your salvation' (Luke 2). If I rejoice in the salvation of God, then my mouth will be enlarged. That is, through meditation on the word of God one comes to the lifting of the heart, hence: 'Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians, our heart is enlarged' (2 Corinthians 5). From the breadth of the heart wisdom is supplied to the mouth.
2.2: 2.2 There is none holy. Rabanus. Beside you, Lord, because no one is made so except by you, and although there are those who are called many gods and many lords, none of them is by nature what God is; because he alone is the one who says: 'I am who am' (Exodus 3). For a shadow is nothing in comparison with a body, or smoke in comparison with fire. As the Lord is. The same. It does not say 'except the Lord': but there is none like the Lord, holy and sanctifying, just and justifying.
2.3: 2.3 Do not. She rebukes the Jews and the wise of the world, exalting themselves against the knowledge of God. Solomon: 'Seek not things higher than yourself,' and elsewhere: 'God is in heaven, and you upon earth: let your words be few.' Old things, etc. Things that pertain to the old man, that is, to the carnal way of life, inquire into knowledge, which is only from God: because he is the Lord of knowledges, in whom are all the treasures of wisdom. Are prepared for him. Because he removes himself from thoughts that are without understanding, or thoughts are prepared for him, that is, made manifest. Hence: 'The Lord knows the thoughts of men.' The God of knowledges. Rabanus, as above. He knows you, etc., up to 'and they are not from him from whom men are.'
2.4: 2.4 Rabanus. That is, the intention of those who seem to themselves powerful, as though they could fulfil the divine commandments without God's help. And the weak. Rabanus. Those who trust in the piety of God say: 'Have mercy on me, O God, for I am weak' (Psalm 6). The Gentile people was weak when a stranger to the testament of God, but now girded with strength, when clothed with the shield of faith and the helmet of salvation and the sword of the spirit, it will be able to quench the fiery darts of the devil.
2.5: 2.5 They that were full before have hired themselves out for bread. The Jews, filled before, namely with the mysteries of the oracles, hired themselves out for bread, that is, separated themselves from God, or were torn from their own seats, that they might not receive the Gospel, which deals with the bread that came down from heaven. The same were filled who were also mighty, that is, the Israelites to whom the oracles of God were entrusted, but the son of the handmaid, they were diminished, who withdrew themselves and did not believe in the Savior, and in the very bread, that is, the divine oracles, tasted only earthly things. But the Gentiles, to whom the law was not given, after they came through the New Testament to those oracles, hungering much passed over the earth, because in them they savored not earthly but heavenly things. In the Greek thus: The full were diminished with bread, and the hungry passed over the earth. And the hungry. That is, the Gentiles, before needy, now taste the bread of the word of God, for it is sweet. So long were they fed with the knowledge of God. The barren has borne. In the number seven the whole Church is designated, hence John also writes to seven churches, showing that he writes to the fullness of one; hence: 'Wisdom has built herself a house, she has set up seven pillars' (Proverbs 9). The Church was barren among the Gentiles before this offspring which we see arose. We also see the earthly Jerusalem, once fruitful, now weakened: because whoever were sons in her were free by her power; but now, there, since it is the letter and the spirit is not, her power lost, she is weakened. Rabanus. 'Very many' in the Hebrew and in the Septuagint it has 'seven.' The Jews say that when Samuel was born, the firstborn son of Phenenna died, and as each of Anna's sons was born, each of Phenenna's died. But Phenenna had seven; Anna five. But the Hebrews count the two sons of Samuel among Anna's sons. The same. The barren, etc., up to 'we have been enriched by this her poverty.'
2.7: 2.7 The poor, etc. Jesus, who for our sake became poor, and enriches the same with the glory of the resurrection.
2.8: 2.8 From the dust. From corruption, Christ, hence: 'Nor will you give your holy one to see corruption' (Psalm 15). From the dung. Rabanus, as above. The Jewish people, among whom the Apostle, having said that he persecuted the Church, says: 'What things were gain to me, I counted dung [loss] for Christ' (Philippians 3). With princes. The same. To whom it is said: 'You shall sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel' (Matthew 25). The throne of glory. Sitting in the equity of the Father, both because the Father gave all judgment to the Son, and because of his kingdom there will be no end (John 5). The poles of the earth. The four regions of the world, namely, in which he extended the circle of the Church, who from the rising of the sun to its setting praise the name of the Lord (Psalm 112). Mystically, the preachers, upon whom the world, that is the Church, is established by their faith, of whom it is said: 'Under whom they stoop that bear up the world' (Job 9).
2.10: 2.10 They shall fear the Lord. Because he will make his adversary weak. From the ambiguous Greek it can also be understood as 'and his adversary.' For when the Lord begins to possess us, our adversary becomes his; and he is conquered by us, not by our strength, because 'not by his own strength is man mighty.' They shall fear the Lord. The Jewish adversaries, over whom in the heavens, that is the apostles, the Lord thundered, when he terrified them by threatening Gehenna, confirming the threats by signs: hence many were converted. Or they will fear in judgment him whom they despised here while opposing, over whom he will thunder, saying: 'Depart into everlasting fire' (Matthew 25). That this may not befall all, the Lord daily thunders in the heavens, that is in the Scriptures and doctors. In the heavens. Rabanus. Because a just retribution will be on the day of judgment, but meanwhile he thunders from his clouds, which he filled with the Holy Spirit after he ascended the heavens. The ends. The last end of man: because those things will not be judged which in the meantime are changed for better or worse, but the last things in which he is found. And he will give. That is, to Christ, Dominion. That is the Church, hence: 'I will give you the nations for your inheritance.' Or dominion, that is the power of judging, because he gave all judgment to the Son. To his king. Rabanus. To the Christian people, to whom he gives power to rule the flesh, that in him it may overcome the world, who for him shed his blood. Of his Christ. Rabanus, on the books of Kings. Of the Christian people, anointed with chrism: yet the whole body with its head is one Christ. Anna, mother of Samuel, prophesied this, in whom was then figured the change of the old priesthood, and now fulfilled, when the fruitful one was weakened, so that the barren one might have a new priesthood in Christ.
2.12: 2.12 Heli. The same. Interpreted 'stranger,' for he is a stranger to God who does not correct those under him. Ophni, 'disgrace of conversion,' and rightly he is so called who delays to be converted for the better. Phinees, 'hardening of the mouth,' or 'sparing the mouth.' We read of two priests Phinees: one just, the son of Eleazar, the other unjust, the son of Heli. Priests who guard their mouth lest anything perverse go out from it are signified in the son of Eleazar. But those who have a stopped mouth, either by inexperience or by consciousness of sins, are figured by the son of Heli. Rabanus. Josephus relates, etc., up to 'and the fault of subjects will be imputed to them.'
2.19: 2.19 A little tunic. The tunic which Anna made, that is, grace, and handed to the boy, is the beginning doctrine, by which the faithful receive the first rudiments, hence: 'I gave you milk to drink, not meat' (1 Corinthians 3). The linen ephod signifies chastity and continence with good works. For he who desires to minister to the Lord must live chastely and continently and exercise himself in good works.
2.25: 2.25 If he sin. Jerome, as above. One does not sin against a man in the way one sins against God, because to sin against a man, that is against a neighbor, is lighter and more venial. But to sin against God, that is to withdraw from his worship, is a sin of impiety, which is more hardly punished and more slowly forgiven. And when someone sins against a man, by appeasing the man he makes God appeasable to himself. But when someone sins against God, who will pray for him? that is, through whom will he make God propitious to himself? Not that no pardon is to be hoped for those who sin in the divine office: but the penalty is greater and pardon slower for those who offend in things consecrated to God, than if they have injured the neighbor by word or deed, because the greater the glory, the graver the offense
2.27: 2.27 Of your father, etc. Aaron, namely. For who else was in the Egyptian servitude who after the liberation was chosen as priest? Whoever is of his line, when he sees the priesthood of the Christians flourish throughout the world while it is taken from himself, wastes away with grief and sorrow.
2.32: 2.32 A rival. Rabanus. The rival of the house of Heli was the priest Zadok, who received the priesthood when Abiathar was cast out by Solomon. Hence: 'Solomon cast out Abiathar from being priest of the Lord, that the word of the Lord might be fulfilled, which he spoke over the house of Heli' (1 Kings 2).
2.33: 2.33 That they may fail. Rabanus. That there may always be someone of the house of Heli in the house of the Lord who, seeing in the dignity of the priesthood another put in his place and himself deprived, may fail in spirit and waste away. This change of the priesthood was fully completed in Christ, being figured by Samuel: for after Samuel the priests were of the line of Aaron, Zadok and Abiathar and others up to the time of Christ.
2.35: 2.35 And my soul. The same. God does not have a soul, but is said figuratively to have a soul, etc., up to 'hence: And the house of Israel rested after the Lord (1 Kings 7).'
2.36: 2.36 It shall come to pass. The same. This is not said properly of the house of Heli, but of the house of Aaron, from whose line they come and are converted to this day. A morsel. Rabanus. 'The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world' (John 6). Because he had said that he had given foods to the house of Aaron from the victims of the Old Testament, which were the sacrifices of the Jews, he says that a morsel of bread to eat is to be begged, which is the sacrifice of the Christians and the food of souls.
3.1: 3.1 Rabanus, on the books of Kings. Hence in those days there was no manifest vision. For because of the sins of the people and the prelates the Lord did not appear through visions or angelic answers, as he appeared to the fathers.
3.3: 3.3 The lamp. The same. Which burned in the tabernacle before the light of day. For it was extinguished at the light of day, but shone until morning; or this signifies that Heli would remain in blindness until he was utterly extinguished with his offspring, that is, died. Mystically, the blindness of Heli signifies the blindness of the Jews, who did not recognize the Savior present, neither the splendor of his miracles nor his teaching, until the priesthood with the people and the temple was overthrown.
3.11: 3.11 Shall tingle. Rabanus. It is the threat of God upon Heli and upon his house, namely because for the sin of the sons of Heli the house was being deprived of the priesthood of the Lord, hence the ears of the hearers shall tingle with violent astonishment.
3.17: 3.17 These things. It was a proverb among the Hebrews. And the sense is: If you hide from me the evil which the Lord spoke to you about me, may it come upon your head.
3.18: 3.18 And not. Rabanus, on the books of Kings. Because nothing of what the Lord spoke, etc., up to 'he did this for a sure reason of their benefit.'
3.20: 3.20 From Dan. The same. By the borders of Judea he embraces the whole of the people. Dan is a small village at the fourth milestone from Paneas, which is so called to this day: the limit of the province of Judea toward the north, from which the Jordan, bursting forth, took its name from the place. For the Hebrews call a river or stream 'Jor.' Dan is interpreted 'judge' or 'judging.' Bersabee. In the tribe of Judah or of Simeon there is a large village at the twentieth milestone from Hebron, lying toward the south: in which a Roman garrison is stationed: from it the borders of Judea extend as far as Dan. Nor should anyone wonder if he finds cities of Judah in the tribe of Simeon or Benjamin. For the tribe of Judah, strong and warlike, often overcoming adversaries, held the leadership among all the tribes, therefore the lots of the other tribes are counted in its portion, otherwise Scripture makes clear that Simeon dwelt in the midst of the tribe of Judah.
4.1: 4.1 And it came to pass. Israel, 'man seeing God,' or 'strong with God': these are the believers. The Philistines, 'falling by the cup,' namely demons, who, intoxicated by the cup of pride, themselves fell, and hasten to pervert men. Against whom Israel, that is the faithful, lest they yield but overcome, encamp beside the Stone of Help, that is the law of Christ, where the stone, that is Christ, is found, of whom: 'The stone which the builders rejected.' But while the faithful meditate on the law of the Lord, to find God as helper, the Philistines came to Aphec, that is 'new fury,' for then, because the unclean spirits see the faithful press on more in the divine laws, they therefore build sharper and new battles, hence, trusting in their own strength and glorying in human wisdom, and thereby despising the grace of the Gospel, about four thousand, the unclean spirits easily lay low. Beside the stone. The stone of help which Samuel afterward set up as a sign, when the Lord first helped him. Aphec. Rabanus. A place near the village Esron of a city of Israel, where Saul fought in the lot of Asher, and it is interpreted 'new fury' or 'seizing'; for those who deserved the wrath of the Lord were seized by enemies.
4.4: 4.4 And they took. The sons of Israel took the ark to where it was captured. And the faithful from the Jews carried the two testaments to the Gentiles. Of him who sits upon. For there was a tablet upon the ark which the cherubim covered with their wings, where the Lord appeared through an angel and spoke. Cherubim, 'fullness of knowledge,' which is found in Christ and in the two testaments.
4.5: 4.5 With the cry. The great cry is the voice of the preachers strengthened by miracles, brought forth from the two testaments. And it resounded. At the voice of preaching the wise of the world, and the demons also, groaned, believing themselves to be overcome.
4.8: 4.8 From the hand. The Jews worship one God, but the Gentiles speak in their own way.
4.11: 4.11 And the ark. The ark captured by foreigners signifies the testament about to pass to the Gentiles.
4.13: 4.13 And when. Rabanus. Josephus relates this thus, etc., up to 'they received again from the house of Eleazar.'
4.18: 4.18 He fell. And with Heli falling from the pontiff's seat the seat remains empty, and the glory of the priests is extinguished. He died. Heli dies, the sons die also, because the pontificate fails with the old priesthood.
4.19: 4.19 The wife. The wife of the priest did not perish before she bore a child to her husband; nor did the synagogue perish wholly before the primitive Church, which was from her, believed.
4.20: 4.20 At that very time. It is figured by an evident sign, because, the carnal priesthood of the Jews being extinguished, the carnal synagogue that adhered to it carnally is extinguished. Fear not. Believers console the synagogue, but, despairing, she does not at all take heed, nor does she reckon the new offspring to glory but to ignominy. Hence follows:
4.21: 4.21 And she called. Chabod, glory; Ichabod, the glory is fallen. For the glory was transferred when the ark was captured, hence: 'The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation yielding its fruits.'
5.1: 5.1 Rabanus, as above. Which is also Asdod, one of the five cities of the Philistines, assigned indeed to the tribe of Judah, but not retained, because it could not expel the natives. It is interpreted 'fire of the father' or 'burning.' The place where the idol Dagon was is well so named, because the coming of the ark to Azotus was a burning of the devil, father of all enemies or wicked ones. Dagon, which is interpreted 'fish of sorrow,' signifies the devil, who in the sea of this world devours sinners, and who is also called Leviathan and Behemoth in Job (Job 40). Azotus. It is the place in which Samuel set up the stone (1 Kings 7), as is shown in what follows.
5.4: 5.4 The head. The pride of the devil, who is the beginning of all sin (Sirach 10). Upon. Rabanus. It signifies the predetermined end at which idolatry would cease. For the threshold is the end of the journey.
5.5: 5.5 The trunk. They found only the back with all the limbs broken, which expresses the flight of idolatry. For he who flees gives his back to the pursuer, hence: 'For you will make them turn their back' (Psalm 20).
5.7: 5.7 And through. Those who receive the testament of God and love the hinder parts of this life will justly be tormented in the hinder parts through these very things, which they ought to reckon as dung. For those who take up the testament of God and, looking back, do not strip themselves of the old vanity are like those who set the ark of the testament beside their idols. And old things indeed fall even against their will, because all flesh is grass. But the ark remains forever, the sure testament of the kingdom of heaven, where the word of God is forever.
5.8: 5.8 Let it be carried about. So that if it goes wherever it will the stroke may accompany it, we may know that the plague is from God, since by the will of God it was done by their counsel, so that the plague might be common, because the guilt was common.
6.5: 6.5 Five golden anuses, etc. Rabanus. The five golden anuses, etc., up to 'is true sorrow and perpetual barrenness.'
6.7: 6.7 A cart. The cross of Christ; the ark, sacred Scripture. Two cows. Isidore. The cows carrying the ark signify the saints, who renounce the world, who have drawn no yoke of transgression. For as cows do not stray from the straight way through affection for their calves, so the holy fathers do not wander from their good purpose by such affection.
6.12: 6.12 Which leads, etc. Rabanus. Namely, going by the royal road to Bethsames, that is, to the house of the sun, the heavenly Jerusalem, where the sun of justice always shines. Bethsames. The same. It is a priestly city in the tribe of Benjamin, which is shown to this day to those going from Eleutheropolis to Nicopolis, at ten miles toward the east: another Bethsames is in the tribe of Naphtali, in which the ancient worshipers remained.
6.13: 6.13 And not. The same. That is, they were neither lifted up by prosperity, etc., up to 'let it be relaxed in weeping.' Bethsames. House of the sun. This is the Church illumined by the sun of justice. For the Bethsamites to reap grain in the valley is for the doctors of the Church to handle the provision of the word of God in humility. The stone in the field of Joshua, Christ in his Church. The wood of the cart, the cross of Christ. To sacrifice the cows upon the stone is to mortify those converted from the world in imitation of Christ.
6.17: 6.17 Azotus one. Jerome, as above. The five cities gave five anuses and five mice. But the remaining cities of the provinces and the villages which were without a wall gave only mice, hence: 'From the walled city to the village that was without a wall,' etc.
6.18: 6.18 Abel. It is a city on the border of Israel, which was called Bethsames before, now called Abel: either because of the mourning made there over the Bethsamite men, or to distinguish the city from Beth-maacah, about which the wise woman cried out to Joab: 'Let those who ask, ask in Abela' (2 Kings 20).
6.19: 6.19 He struck, etc. Who, though they were not Levites, dared to look at the ark. To keep this from happening, in Exodus the people stood far off, Moses alone went up to the Lord. He struck, etc. Jerome. In the Hebrew it is: And he struck of the people seventy men: and fifty thousand men, seventy men, the judges. Septuagint. The Hebrews say that it was lawful for none to see the uncovered ark except the pontiff: they were struck, therefore, because they were unworthy, or had approached unworthily, or had not guarded the ark.
6.21: 6.21 And they sent. Rabanus. The transfer of the testament of the Lord from the Jews to the Gentiles is signified, because, as they defiled the law with carnal observance and the superstitions of the Pharisees, they rejected the teaching of Christ and his disciples; hence: 'It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you, but since you judged yourselves unworthy, behold we turn to the Gentiles' (Acts 13). Cariathiarim. The same. Interpreted 'village of woods,' of which it is said: 'Until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob. Behold, we heard of it in Ephrata, we found it in the fields of the wood' (Psalm 131). For the place of the Lord is the tabernacle of the breast of the Christian people. A city of woods, that is, an assembly of the nations, is a fitting place to receive the ark. In the house of Aminadab, which is interpreted 'my father is willing,' and can say, willingly, namely to you. The same. Cariathiarim is a city of the woodlands, one of the cities of the Gabaonites belonging to the tribe of Judah, at the ninth milestone for those going from Aelia to Diospolis: from it was the prophet Urias whom Joachim killed in Jerusalem, as Jeremiah writes.
7.1: 7.1 Gabaa. Rabanus. 'Hill,' of the souls of the humble, hence: 'Let the mountains receive peace for the people,' etc., that is, the greater mountains the souls, the lesser hills. Or Gabaa is also interpreted 'loftiness,' where Eleazar the priest is appointed. Eleazar. The same. 'Help of God.' Well is he who is called by this name chosen to guard the ark of the Lord, because holy men attribute whatever good they have to God, not to themselves. Hence: 'Our sufficiency is from God, who has made us fit ministers of the New Testament' (2 Corinthians 3).
7.2: 7.2 It was the twentieth year, when in the seventh year of the reign of Saul it was brought into the camp from Cariathiarim. The twentieth year. Rabanus. It is not to be understood so, etc., up to 'because there is no fellowship of light with darkness.'
7.6: 7.6 Masphath. It is a city in the tribe of Judah near Cariathiarim. Rabanus. Masphath: 'watching' or 'contemplation,' etc., up to 'and sees them intent on the love of the heavenly homeland.' And they drew water, etc. So that, as water poured out does not return, neither might they themselves return to idolatry.
7.9: 7.9 A sucking lamb. The lamb offered for the people of God gives victory, and by the passion of Christ, the demons overcome, peace is given to the faithful. Rabanus. An innocent life kindled with the fire of charity. Rabanus. When the Lord thunders through the preachers of the Gospel, the spiritual enemies are put to flight before Israel, that is the people of God, and are pursued by them as far as the house of knowledge: until, namely, every error is purged away and God is truly known.
7.11: 7.11 Bethchar. The same. House of knowledge, or house of the lamb.
7.12: 7.12 And he set it. Another edition: between the new and the old Masphath, and he called its name Abenezer, or Abongener, that is, the stone of help. This is the middle of the Savior, through which one must pass from the old Masphath to the new, that is, from the intention by which false blessedness is awaited in a carnal kingdom, to the intention by which through the New Testament true blessedness is awaited in the kingdom of heaven, than which since nothing is better, thus far God helps. Masphath, the intention of those sitting. The stone between these, Christ, placed between the intention of the Old Testament and the preaching of the Gospel: the stone itself, for the firmness of help, because he helps his own fighting against the demons. Thus far has he helped. Because those who pass these bounds, like heretics, do not deserve the help of God.
7.14: 7.14 And it was. Christ is our peace, who made both one, through whom those who were far off are made near.
7.16: 7.16 Galgala. It is a city where Joshua circumcised the people a second time and celebrated the Passover, and when the manna ceased, Israel used wheaten bread, where also the stones were carried from the bed of the Jordan, where the tabernacle of the testimony was for a long time. It fell to the lot of Judah: and to this day the place is shown at the second milestone from Jericho, venerable to the men of that region. But some suppose another Galgala near Bethel. Galgala is interpreted 'rolling' or 'revelation.' Well, then, the prophet judged Israel in Bethel and in Galgala and in Masphath, and returning to Ramatha to his house he judged Israel there; and he built there an altar to the Lord, giving an example that judgment is to be made in the house of God, not indiscriminately or with a malevolent mind, but according as Scripture has revealed, and with good intention and brotherly love, and that we should so return to Ramatha, to our house, that is, to the inner things of the breast, that we may be free for contemplation, and on the altar of faith offer acceptable victims of work and truth.
7.17: 7.17 He also built there, etc. The law commanded that an altar not be built except where the Lord had chosen; but lest they sacrifice to idols, he built an altar, in which he is not reproved.
8.1: 8.1 It came to pass, etc., he set his sons. Rabanus, on the books of Kings, vol. 2. Because according to Josephus he set one in Bethlehem, another in Bersabee.
8.2: 8.2 Abia. The same. 'Father is Lord,' or 'he was father.' Well, then, those who did not remain in justice once begun, and neglected the fatherhood of the Lord. 'God was' or 'Father was' they were named, to signify they were unworthy of the fatherhood of God.
8.3: 8.3 And they did not walk. Because for a gift they oppressed justice, turning aside to feasts and costly banquets.
9.2: 9.2 By the name of Saul. Rabanus, on the books of Kings, vol. 2. Saul, who, God being offended, was made king over Israel, etc., up to 'and became turbulent from his own pleasure.' The same. That Saul, seeking his father's she-asses, came to the prophet by whom he was anointed signifies that the Jews, following the folly of carnal sense, seek the luxury of the world through devious errors; for the ass is a brutish and lustful animal. And coming to the prophet, that is Moses, they hear that the she-asses have been found, that is, that the goods of the earth are owed to them, by whom also the oil of anointing and the helm of the kingdom is promised, in which for a time they would rescue their brethren from the hand of enemies. The same. According to the justice of the present life. The same. This pertains more to Christ, of whom it is said: 'Behold my servant, whom I have chosen' (Isaiah 44). And elsewhere: 'Who among the sons of God is like God?' (Psalm 86). Staters. A stater is a shekel which has twenty obols, that is, ten denarii.
9.7: 9.7 Let us give to the man. Although they had decided to give, we do not read that Samuel received it; yet if he had received it, it would not be reckoned a reward for divination, but the stipend of a prophet.
9.9: 9.9 Formerly in Israel. As Bede says, these are not the words of the historian but of Esdras. Seer. A prophet is so called because through the Spirit he foreknows the future.
9.11: 9.11 The slope, etc., going out to draw water. A slope is a winding ascent of a mountain.
9.16: 9.16 And you shall anoint him as leader. Saul anointed signifies Christ, who himself is also called Christ; hence: 'Why were you not afraid to put forth your hand against the Lord's anointed?' (2 Kings 1).
9.19: 9.19 All that. Rabanus. The Hebrews report that it was in Saul's heart that he would be king, since he had seen in a vision that he was placed at the top of a palm tree, which is a sign of one who will reign.
9.22: 9.22 Taking him thus. That Samuel led Saul to the high place and gave him refreshment signifies the prophets calling the people of the Hebrews by their teaching to higher things, that, refreshed by spiritual knowledge, they may stand on the summit of virtues and not fall back into vices. Dining room. An upper room, from the three couches of those reclining.
9.24: 9.24 On purpose, that is, by Providence, it is given to be understood that he had already eaten, though not fully, because, the Lord having revealed that Saul would come, the banquet was postponed.
9.27: 9.27 And as they were going down. They went down from the high place so that he might speak in some more secret place about the kingdom and anoint him.
10.1: 10.1 And he took. The little flask is a four-cornered earthen vessel, having a hole in its side, by which the fragility of the kingdom is designated.
10.6: 10.6 And you shall prophesy with them. The Jews hold that he prophesied about the age to come, about Gog and Magog, about the rewards of the just and the punishments of the wicked.
10.7: 10.7 When therefore. As if to say: by these signs you will be able to know that God has willed you to be king. Therefore act royally in all things, because the Lord is with you.
10.8: 10.8 Seven days, understood: in the consecration of your kingdom, as in the consecration of priests victims were offered for seven days.
10.10: 10.10 And they came. It signifies that all that Moses and the prophets foretold has come to pass for the Jews. They, holding the books of the law and the prophets, seem to prophesy, when they are known to proclaim the future mysteries of Christ and the Church written in them.
10.12: 10.12 And who. As if to say: who is greater than he in dignity and wisdom? He can therefore be among the prophets as father and master. And who is their father, that is of the prophets, understood: but God. Mystically, the elders of Israel, having rejected Samuel, asked a king for themselves, and the scribes with the Pharisees, having rejected Christ the true priest, cried out: 'We have no king but Caesar' (John 19); hence Samuel is interpreted: 'his name is God'; Saul, 'asked for' or 'petition,' who was demanded by the people, is understood as Barabbas. Cis, 'hard' or 'vomiting'; Abiel, 'my father is God'; for the Jews, hard and vomiting, by confessing God the Father, deny the Son; but he who denies the Son denies also the Father who sent him (1 John 2). Saul, seeking his father's she-asses, was taken up to the kingdom. The Savior, sent by the Father to the sheep that had perished of the house of Israel, was established as king over all the people. For there are as many she-asses as sheep. Saul received the shoulder, and Christ the principality (Matthew 15). Saul was anointed by Samuel, and the Only-begotten was anointed by the Father with spiritual anointing. In number Saul stood above, because our head is Christ, who is over us (1 Corinthians 11).
11.1: 11.1 Rabanus. Jabes, 'sense'; Galaad, 'heap of witness.' Naas, that is 'serpent,' namely the devil, goes up against the sense instructed in the witness of Scripture.
11.2: 11.2 And he answered. The war of Naas signifies the war of the heretics against the Church. Naas is interpreted 'serpent'; Ammon, 'pressing' or 'narrowing,' or 'people of sorrow.' Jabes, 'dried up'; Galaad, 'heap of witness'; Naas therefore signifies the ancient serpent, who is prince of the Ammonites, that is the heretics. For this is the people of sorrow, who have not the joy of the Holy Spirit, who sets a covenant with the people of the Church to put out the right eyes, namely the sight of sound orthodox faith. He leaves the left eye, that is, that they may perceive only perverse things. But the mind of the faithful, dried from the filth of vices, gathers the heap of witness, that is the knowledge of Holy Scripture, with which it may manfully resist the enemy.
11.8: 11.8 In Bezech. Rabanus, on the books of Kings, vol. 2. The city, namely Adonibezec, etc., up to 'the Church spreads through the whole world.'
11.11: 11.11 They were scattered. Because the gathering of the perverse is not joined by unity of charity and faith, it is separated from one another by dissension; hence: 'Your enemies, O Lord, shall perish and be scattered' (Psalm 91).
12.17: 12.17 The wheat harvest. Rabanus. Namely the gathering of the Gentile people to the faith. Voices. That is, thunder and rains. It is not the custom of Judea to rain in summertime.
13.1: 13.1 The son of one year, etc. Rabanus. By anticipation he speaks of Ishbosheth, the son of Saul, etc., up to 'and had not judged the people during his whole life as others did.'
13.2: 13.2 Gabaa. The same. It is the city of Phinees, the son of Eleazar, etc., up to 'the men remaining with Saul, Catholics firmly adhering to Christ.'
13.6: 13.6 They hid themselves in caves. The same. Those hidden, namely, etc., up to 'joined themselves with their own in battle.'
13.13: 13.13 You have done foolishly, and not. The same. It seems to some that Saul sacrificed blamelessly, etc., up to 'and therefore he is rightly blamed and charged with folly.' Had you not done so. Eucherius, on the books of Kings, from Augustine. It is not to be taken as though the Lord had prepared Saul to reign forever and had not wished to keep this for him when he sinned: for he knew he would sin. But he had prepared his kingdom, in which there would be a figure of the eternal kingdom, hence he added: And now your kingdom shall not stand. What was signified in him therefore stood and will stand; but it will not stand for this man, because he was not to reign forever; nor his offspring, so that at least through descendants, succeeding one another, what was said, forever, might seem fulfilled.
13.14: 13.14 But by no means. The rejection of Saul, the taking away of the kingdom of the Jews. David his survivor, Christ about to succeed the people of the Jews. He has sought for himself. Not as though not knowing where he is, but speaks through a man after the manner of men, because by speaking so he also seeks us. For not only for God the Father, but for the Only-begotten himself, who came to seek what had perished, we were not yet such that we were chosen in him before the foundation of the world. He will therefore seek for himself, he said: he will have his own; hence in the Latin tongue this verb takes a preposition, and is said 'to acquire'; which is plain enough. Without the preposition also 'to seek' is understood as 'to acquire,' from which gains are called 'quaestus.' A man after his heart. He signifies David, or the Mediator of the New Testament himself, who was figured in the chrism with which David was anointed, and his offspring. Rabanus. The devil also through the pagans, etc., up to 'but we inquire into the future.'
14.1: 14.1 Jonathan. 'Gift of the dove.' These are those who are filled with the gift of the Holy Spirit, through whom the Lord scatters the assemblies of heretics and puts them to flight. His armor-bearer, the disciples of spiritual men, who take the way not over level ground but over steep: because priests cannot go against enemies unless, walking by the narrow way, they advance between the two Testaments, and between prosperity and adversity, as between two crags on right and left, and climb to the heights of contemplation with the whole effort of the mind. Jonathan crosses to the enemies only when provoked: because Catholics do not stir up contention against heretics unless first provoked to the struggle. Jonathan therefore lays enemies low in the field of cultivation: and doctors conquer heretics in the meditation of Scripture.
14.27: 14.27 But Jonathan. 'Gift of the dove.' He signifies those who, having received the grace of the Holy Spirit, prepare to spurn the allurements of the world. For he cannot fight manfully against the spiritual Philistines, that is the demons, who does not know how to turn aside from the sweetness of the world. They were enlightened. Rabanus, from Eucherius. Not for seeing, etc., up to 'and to need the prayers of the brethren.'
14.33: 14.33 The people had sinned against the Lord by eating. Rabanus. To have sinned against the Lord, etc., up to 'and to have eaten with the blood.'
14.34: 14.34 Slay upon this, etc. So that the blood may flow to the ground. Or he ate with the blood, because they ate before the evening sacrifice, which after a slaughter was customary to be done before food. Or in this they sinned, as some prefer, that they did not lead their victims to the door of the tabernacle. And they slew. The slaying of animals is baptism, in which the old man dies. The huge rock, on which the slaughter was done, is faith, without which the old man does not die. The slaughter on the ground, the baptism of heretics. Whose blood they eat, when they gather to themselves the washed without purification of sins. These animals taken from the Philistines signify either those brought back from heretics, or those converted from paganism: the unskilled rebaptize the former; the latter they baptize otherwise than the Church hands down. Whom Christ, like Saul in his faith, as upon a great rock, commanded the oxen and sheep, that is the varieties of men, to be baptized, to be slain.
14.35: 14.35 Then he first began to build an altar to the Lord, etc. Because obediently and rightly. But above, when he was rebuked by Samuel, he is not said to have built for the Lord, because he built disobediently.
14.38: 14.38 Bring hither all the corners of the people. He calls the princes the corners of the people, to whom on either side the people clung as walls to corners.
14.44: 14.44 May God do so. An oath of the Hebrews, which is understood by its opposite, as if he said: May the evil that is due to you be imputed to me, if I do not kill you.
14.45: 14.45 Who has done. Past good deeds help much. For unless Jonathan's past goods had helped him, he would not have escaped the evils that threatened. For God is not unjust, that he should forget good deeds.
15.1: 15.1 And he said, etc. The ox, etc. Rabanus, on the books of Kings, vol. 2. Therefore the Lord commands the beasts of Amalec to be destroyed, etc., up to 'they cast the mockery of God into heaven.'
15.6: 15.6 Saul said to the Cinite. The same. The Cinite is Jethro himself, kinsman of Moses, etc., up to 'the multitude of the people.'
15.11: 15.11 It repents me. Gregory, on the books of Kings. By this rebuke the pride of the king is cast out, etc., up to 'that we may ascend to greater things, and always from humility.'
15.17: 15.17 Was it not when. Gregory, Morals book 34, and in Eucherius. He is little in his own eyes, etc., up to 'hence: They have made you leader; be not lifted up, but be as one of them.'
15.22: 15.22 Better is, etc. Rabanus, on the books of Kings. Because by victims another's flesh, etc., up to 'but Paul says boldly: I am ready not only to be bound in Jerusalem but also to die (Acts 21).'
15.26: 15.26 I will not return. The same. Another edition, etc., up to 'here he threatens and does not abide.'
15.27: 15.27 But he. As in the passion of the Lord the high priest rent his garment, so also Saul rent the garment of the prophet. For through both powers, the royal and the priestly, the rending that was made shows that the kingdom of the Jews and the priesthood cannot stand, because they refused to receive the true king and priest, that is Christ. Rabanus, from Augustine. This man to whom he said, etc., up to 'not according to the one and same nature of the human race.'
15.28: 15.28 He rent. Although he afterward reigned forty years, yet then he deserved to be torn from his stock, and handed over to a better, that is David, and from Saul, that is the Jews, the kingdom is taken away and handed to Christ. He corrects the king for disobedience, because he did not fulfil the command of the Lord, and foretells the loss of the kingdom. Rightly does he lose the kingdom who does not know how to hold it. But he rules well who obeys his superior and puts his authority before his inferiors.
15.33: 15.33 And into pieces. When some read in the Scriptures that the saints spare none of the enemies, they call them cruel, and do not understand the mysteries foreshadowed in these words: that, fighting against vices, we leave none at all. For if we spare, it will be reckoned to us as guilt, as to Saul, who kept the king of Amalec alive. But the saints, like Samuel, leave no sin unpunished.
16.7: 16.7 Look not. The elder sons of Jesse being rejected, the least is chosen for the kingdom, because the Jewish priesthood and the kingdom of the former people being scorned, Christ, head of the lesser people, was made king and priest.
16.11: 16.11 The little one. From the care of flocks David was made king of men: Christ, from the sheepfold of the Jewish people, was transferred to the kingdom of the Gentiles. Gregory, Morals, book 1, chapter 6; book 18, chapter 6. The devil, though he always desires the affliction of the just, etc., up to 'power is only from God.'
16.16: 16.16 One skilled in playing the harp, etc. Rabanus, from Eucherius. David was skilled in songs of music, etc., up to 'as by the sweetness of the harp he is recalled by the tranquillity of our speech.'
16.23: 16.23 Saul was refreshed. For before he was vexed by the demon even to suffocation. Boethius reports that a certain philosopher drove a demon from a possessed body by the touch of the harp.
17.1: 17.1 Gathering. Rabanus, on the books of Kings. Azeca. It is a city of the Canaanites in the tribe of Judah to which Joshua pursued the five kings, and today it is called the village Azeca between Eleutheropolis and Aelia, which is interpreted 'strength' and 'snare.' Dommim. It is a village in the tribe of Judah on the borders of Eleutheropolis, distant from it twenty-seven miles. Dommim is interpreted 'silence' or 'joy.'
17.2: 17.2 Of the terebinth. A terebinth is in Sichem, under which Jacob hid the idols near Neapolis.
17.4: 17.4 A bastard. Because he was born of an ignoble father and a noble mother.
17.12: 17.12 Eight sons. Jerome, Hebrew Questions, vol. 3. In Paralipomenon only seven are mentioned, etc., up to 'Isidore also says the prophet Nathan was of the Gabaonites.'
17.14: 17.14 David. And the eighth, who is chosen for the kingdom, this is Christ, who emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2), because by the glory of the resurrection he also obtained the kingdom among the Gentiles.
17.21: 17.21 For Israel had set up the battle line, but the Philistines. The fight of the Philistines against Israel can be taken as the fight of the demons against the Church. Goliath signifies the pride of the devil: which David, that is Christ, laid low in single combat and rescued the people of God. He who slew the lion and the bear, that is, the devil and Antichrist, the one now lying in ambush secretly, the other afterward raging openly. Pride challenged humility, the devil Christ. David took the arms of war, which for his age and small stature he could not carry, and cast them off. He took five stones from the brook and put them in the shepherd's bag: armed with these he conquered. So Christ, at the time of the revelation of the New Testament, to suggest and commend grace, laid aside the bodily sacraments of the law, which were not imposed on the Gentiles, which we read in the old law and do not observe, but understand as sent before and set down for some signification: these he laid aside as the burdens of the law, and took up the law itself. For the five stones signify the five books of Moses. He took five stones from the brook, that is from this world. For the mortal world glides by. The stones were as if in a brook in the first people. There they lay idle and profited nothing. The river passed above. But David received grace, so that the law might be useful, which cannot be fulfilled without grace. For 'charity is the fulfilling of the law' (Romans 13). Because therefore grace causes the law to be fulfilled, grace is signified by milk, that is, what is gratuitous in the flesh; where the mother seeks not to receive but to give, she gives freely and is grieved if there is none to receive. David showed that the law cannot work without grace; wishing to join those five stones, by which the law in the five books is signified, to grace, he put them in the shepherd's bag, in which milk was usually drawn. Armed with these he went out against the proud one. He took one stone and cast one, struck him on the forehead and he fell, from that place of the body where he did not have the sign of Christ. He took five, he sent one. Five books were chosen, but unity conquers. The fullness of the law is therefore charity, as the Apostle says. 'Bearing with one another in love, careful to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace' (Ephesians 4). When he was cast down, he took away the sword and cut off his head. Christ slew the devil from his own members, when the magi believed, whom he had in his hand and through whom he slew others, turning their tongues against the devil, and so the head of Goliath is cut off with his own sword.
17.28: 17.28 I know your pride and the wickedness of your heart, because. Rabanus. He thought there was swelling in him on account of the anointing by Samuel, as though from it he had taken boldness, and feared that if he engaged the Philistine he would be killed. Hence he adds, You came down to see the battle, that is, you appear proud in this, that though you have no custom of fighting, you inquire into the acts of battle like a soldier.
17.29: 17.29 Is there not a cause? The same. As if he said, There is, because it is not a wish to fight, but that I might know what I did not know. Yet he had taken boldness from this, that he had received the Holy Spirit; having experienced God's help against the lion and the bear, and therefore boldly offered himself for single combat, not so much desirous of victory as an avenger of the blasphemies against God and the injuries of the people.
17.41: 17.41 And he went. Rabanus, on the books of Kings. Allegorically, the Philistines are demons, etc., up to 'as Goliath, lifted up, they cut off with his own sword.'
17.51: 17.51 And he took. Rabanus, from Gregory. The Catholic man also gathers the testimony of Scripture, etc., up to 'we conquer heretics with their own sentences.' The head. David took the head of the Philistine to Jerusalem to terrify them, who, trusting in the strength and height of their walls, thought themselves unconquerable, that they might not doubt that they were to be conquered by him.
17.55: 17.55 Of whom. Augustine. The reason Saul and Abner did not know David, though he had lived with them a good while, was the beard, which had grown on the youth while he was absent. Lives. Rabanus. Like this is the saying: 'Naboth blessed God and the king.' 'Because your soul lives not, O king, if I know,' or 'let me see your death if I know.' 'If' also is sometimes put for 'not,' according to the saying: 'If they shall enter into my rest' (Psalm 92), that is, 'they shall not enter,' hence it is plain it is explained thus: 'If I know,' that is, 'I do not know.'
18.1: 18.1 And it came to pass, etc., and loved, etc. Rabanus, on the books of Kings. Jonathan loved David: a warlike man, that is, a youth fit for battles. Jonathan signifies those of the Jews who believed in Christ and, having received the grace of the Holy Spirit, left all things for Christ and followed him. Hence Peter: 'Behold, we have left all things and followed you' (Matthew 19). For so Jonathan gave David his garments, from the tunic to the belt, when believers brought into the service of Christ all they had.
18.7: 18.7 Saul has slain, etc. This was the seedbed of hatred against David. So the Jews, hearing Christ whom they had crucified preached in the churches, and the victory by which he conquered the ancient enemy and believers rejoicing in his praise, took it heavily. Saul a thousand. Namely those who were slain in flight. David ten thousand. Namely the Philistine, who, one being cast down, put all to flight.
18.10: 18.10 And he held. So while Christ preached the Gospel, the Jews strove to bring death. But while he withdrew for the salvation of the Gentiles, they only harmed themselves.
18.17: 18.17 And Saul said. Isidore, on the books of Kings, vol. 5, chapter 11. Saul, a cunning pretender, was eager to bind David to Michal his daughter, etc., up to 'he is recalled by the tranquillity of speech.'
18.27: 18.27 He slew, etc., and brought, etc. Rabanus. So Christ was first glorified among the Gentiles, when he would join the Synagogue to himself, and first cut away uncleanness among the Gentiles. For when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel shall be saved (Romans 11).
19.3: 19.3 In the field, etc. Where he had been accustomed to come for the sake of consoling, where it had been agreed that David should be killed.
19.11: 19.11 Saul sent therefore. Rabanus. This pertains not to the cross of Christ but to the passion, etc., up to 'they persecute him as a sinner.'
19.13: 19.13 A skin. From it a pillow was sewn, which, with unshorn hair, would feign the head of a man wrapped up in the bed.
19.18: 19.18 In Ramatha. The city of Saul is in the tribe of Benjamin at the sixth milestone from Aelia toward the north, facing Bethel; another Ramatha is in the tribe of Asher. These names fit well with the deeds themselves, because the sayings of the prophets have both the loftiness of knowledge and the beauty of eloquence.
19.21: 19.21 He sent a third time, etc. He went, etc. Rabanus. Saul and his messengers also signify the Jews, who, while they desire to oppose Christ, have in their mouth the sacraments of the law and the prophets for the testimony of Christ, and dispute with the Church about the Scriptures as with prophets, as those prophesied with the prophets.
19.24: 19.24 He prophesied. These prophets were religious men, called Nazarites, who did not drink wine and were always at leisure, singing hymns and psalms. Naked. The Jews also, stripped of faith and of the priesthood and kingdom, have the law and the prophets in their mouth. Is Saul also. It is called a proverb, which often is in the mouth of speakers. For it seemed a marvelous thing that so profane a man should prophesy. And we, when we see the ignorant teach, rightly say, Is Saul also among the prophets? Rabanus. A great question arises here, etc., up to 'but is to be understood only of royal things.' The same. It is likewise asked, etc., up to 'the more they did not make good use of those gifts.'
20.3: 20.3 With one step only. Rabanus. He calls a wall a step, by putting which between himself and the enemies he escaped through a window of the house, where the besiegers were.
20.16: 20.16 And he sought. The same. It is a prolepsis, that is, an anticipation, etc., up to 'but the Lord avenging for him.'
20.17: 20.17 And he added. The same. So that David might be shown to be innocent of the destruction of his enemies, because he loved him according to the law of God. Who, though prevented by death from having an earthly kingdom with him as he hoped, without any doubt received fellowship in the heavenly kingdom with him whom he loved for his virtues, being himself also a man of virtues. Do you not: as if he said, You love my enemy who opposes me, in which you show you were conceived in adulterous intercourse. For those lawfully born love their fathers more closely. Rabanus. What is it that Jonathan, wishing to save David, etc., up to 'but he did not know him whom Moses and the prophets had foretold.'
21.1: 21.1 Achimelech. Rabanus. That is, 'my brother the king,' etc., up to 'the apostles were sanctified by faith from the contagion of the Jews.'
21.5: 21.5 Way. The same. In the Hebrew, etc., up to 'and in the urgent danger of life he would not eat of them.'
21.6: 21.6 He gave him therefore. The same. As far as pertains to prophecy, etc., up to 'hence: If they have persecuted me, they will persecute you also (John 15).'
21.7: 21.7 In the tabernacle of the Lord. Rabanus. In the Hebrew, 'bound in the sight of the Lord,' for perhaps he had vowed that for some days he would stay in the tabernacle of the Lord and be free for prayers. Doeg the Edomite. The same. Who was keeper of camels, that is, of an unfruitful and crooked flock, etc., up to 'because no one can harm Christ, prince of priests, who ascended the heavens victorious.' Rabanus, from Isidore. Achis is interpreted, etc., up to 'within, the divine power lay hidden like a beard.'
22.1: 22.1 When. Rabanus. It signified that our Redeemer, having completed the passion and redemption of the human race, first set the Church from the Israelite people in Judea, from which he also took flesh. Where his brethren, that is, the apostles, and his father's house, that is, those who believed from the Jews, came to him, and all who were in distress assembled to him, etc. To whom, namely, he says: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you (Matthew 11).
22.2: 22.2 In debt. The same. By the account, namely, of sins which they pay to the devil, while they present their members to serve iniquity unto iniquity; it is necessary that such persons do penance in bitterness of mind, and come to David, that is to Christ, desired by all the nations, that he may become their prince. For he is the judge of the living and the dead, and prince of peace, of whose kingdom there will be no end.
22.5: 22.5 And Gad said. The same. Gad is brought in unexpectedly. For no mention is made of him in what precedes, as also of Elijah, where it is said: And Elijah the Tishbite, of the inhabitants of Gilead, said (1 Kings 17). By the mouth of the Lord, therefore, the prophet Gad said to David that he should not tarry among the Gentiles in a polluted land, but return to the land of Judah, where according to the will of the Lord he should endure persecution.
23.11: 23.11 Will he come down. Rabanus. If you remain here, Saul will come down, and the men of Keilah will deliver you into his hand: therefore he declared their will. The men of Keilah, ungrateful for David's benefits, whom he delivered from the hands of the Philistines, signify the unbelief and inconstancy of the Jews, who, ungrateful to their Redeemer, plot with the powers of the world. Keilah is interpreted 'cast by a sling,' or 'excelling in itself.' 'The wicked walk round about' (Psalm 11). And: 'A fool changes like the moon' (Sirach 27).
23.14: 23.14 Ziph. Rabanus. They betrayed David, hiding among them, to Saul, and discussed his death with him. The Ziphites are interpreted 'flourishing' or 'budding,' and signify those Jews who, seeking the flower of an earthly kingdom, consulted with their princes about the death of Christ, how they might seize him, lost through his disciple, and deliver him to the governor to be killed; and the flourishing of the world betray Christ in his members, namely the powers of this world.
24.4: 24.4 And there was there, etc. Rabanus, from Eucherius. A king caught by unforeseen ambushes, etc., up to 'Samuel said: The Lord has rent the kingdom of Israel from your hand.' Gregory, Morals, vol. 2. What is signified by Saul but wicked rulers? etc., up to 'hence Moses, when he knew the people were complaining against him and Aaron, said: For what are we? (Exodus 16).' He lives, etc. Josephus supplies what the letter lacks: those who were with him reproved him. For he was sparing an enemy who wished to destroy him, and he calmed them, saying: The Lord lives, etc.
25.1: 25.1 Pharan. Rabanus, on the books of Kings, vol. 2. It is a town in Arabia near the Saracens, who were in the wilderness: the children of Israel passed through it when they moved camp from Mount Sinai. It is toward the southern region, and is distant from Haila toward the east a journey of three days. Scripture records that Ishmael dwelt in the wilderness of Pharan, from whom come the Ishmaelites, who are now called Saracens. We also read that Chodorlaomor struck those who were in the wilderness of Pharan.
25.3: 25.3 Nabal, etc. Rabanus, same place. A hard and very wicked man, etc., up to 'hence: There will be joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance (Luke 15).'
25.18: 25.18 Seahs. A seah is a kind of measure containing a modius and a half. Polenta is the finest flour. Raisin is what is dried long in the sun before it ripens, and so kept. Cakes of figs, that is, bundles of the fruit of figs.
25.29: 25.29 The soul shall be, etc. Rabanus, from Eucherius. By a most beautiful comparison, etc., up to 'or have been taken from human affairs.'
25.37: 25.37 When he had digested. Gregory. We correct the irascible better if we turn aside at the very stirring of anger; for when troubled they do not know what they hear. But when they return to themselves, they receive the words of exhortation the more willingly, the more they blush at being tolerated so calmly. To a mind drunk with fury everything right that is said seems perverse: hence Abigail praiseworthily kept silent her fault to drunken Nabal, which she praiseworthily told when the wine was digested. For the evil he had done could do harm, because being drunk he did not hear.
25.44: 25.44 To Phalti the son. Rabanus. As the Hebrews report, Phalti did not know her, because if he had known her, David would not afterward have taken her back, because it is forbidden in the law. For Phalti was from Gallim, that is, from cleansing, that is from the law. For he was a teacher of the law from Baurim, that is from the chosen, when Michal was given to him. For Phalti is said to mean 'going' when she is taken away; Phaltiel, that is 'escaping from God,' is said: because he guarded him lest he touch her, lest he become a transgressor of the law: yet he followed her weeping as far as Baurim for joy, because he had not touched her.
26.1: 26.1 And the Ziphites came, etc., Sleeping, etc. Rabanus, on the books of Kings, vol. 2. The Jews persecute Christ, etc., up to 'he ascended to the height of heaven.'
27.8: 27.8 They made raids on the Gessurites, and the Gerzites, etc. Jerome, Hebrew Questions on the books of Kings. These villages were not under the power of Achis. They are said to have been inhabited in the land from of old, because they had been inhabited quiet and secure, and had suffered the attacks of no enemy.
28.3: 28.3 Now Samuel. Rabanus, on the books of Kings, vol. 2. Samuel is read above to be dead: but the cause of his resurrection is repeated, for the condemnation of Saul, who, forsaking God, against the law, consulted the witch.
28.6: 28.6 And he consulted the Lord. Rabanus. As the Hebrews report, an oracle was sought from God by fasting and praying: and God revealed the future to them through dreams, which Saul is not read to have done. Nor by priests. The same. In the Hebrew: Neither by Urim, that is doctrine, nor by the ephod, namely what the priest wore on his breast, on which was written: doctrine and truth.
28.9: 28.9 Magicians. Magicians use human blood and contact with the dead in their sorceries and divinations; soothsayers divine by words alone, that is, by incantations. Apollo, the patron of these arts, is called Pythian, from whom come the Pythonesses, that is, diviners: these Saul removed as though from zeal for the law, because, as they say, compelled by demons they proclaimed that David would be king.
28.11: 28.11 Whom shall I bring up? Augustine, letter to Simplician, vol. 2. You ask whether a malignant spirit could raise the soul of a just man, etc., up to 'so that it is brought back to an equal condition of death, that each was a man and could die; already dead, he foretold death to the living.'
29.5: 29.5 Saul has slain. Those envying David's glory say that he fought only among ten thousands, as of less power, but Saul among thousands, as innumerable, nor do they add how many they slew, envying their praise, or lest they terrify their own. In the oldest books 'thousands' is not found: but as though 'a thousand, and ten thousand only.'
30.1: 30.1 And when the Amalekites. Gregory, Morals book 29. It must be considered what it is that the Amalekites invade Ziklag and take the prey, etc., up to 'whom the world has commonly despised to have.'
30.21: 30.21 They had stayed behind. The two hundred weary men who were left with the baggage signify the weak of the Church, who cannot run with the spiritual men on the way, but because they have faith and keep good work, they receive from Christ the reward of blessedness together with the perfect.
31.2: 31.2 They struck Jonathan, etc. Rabanus, on the books of Kings, vol. 2. Jonathan, Abinadab, etc., up to 'when he perished with his sons.'
31.4: 31.4 Then he took. By the sword with which he spared the Amalekites against God's command, he rightly killed himself: so he who, having received power for the common good, either does not use it or abuses it, without doubt pierces himself with his own sword, and the one by which he should have been defended against the enemy rather helps the enemy.
31.11: 31.11 The inhabitants. Those whom Saul had defended from adversaries repay what they can. Let us also, as far as we can, rescue our benefactors, slain by the sword of sin, from the reproach of the Philistines.
